1.pericope_label: Hear ye this, O house of Jacob, which swear by the name of the LORD, but not in truth nor in righteousness

schools.summary: Narrows the address to the Judaean exiles, reads the roll of honours as sustained irony against men who were not true citizens of Zion, and marks where the summons ends and the divine speech begins.

Explains the reversal of tone from the chapter's opening, allows the profession only as profession, and turns the boast of the holy city on a Jerusalem that had scarcely any holiness left and on those who claim the household of God while strangers to it.
Reduces the profession to name without truth and the reliance to vain confidence, and states the chapter's purpose as leaving no pretext for crediting anything to idols.
Counts the credentials one by one to show how high a profession may soar and how low it may sink, and observes that many who are themselves unholy are proud of their relation to the church.

debates.question: Why is the honourable name used of a people being rebuked?

positions.view: not to speak respectfully but to shame a false boast: the Israel addressed is spurious and has nothing left but the name
the ideal attributes are pressed deliberately against the actual state, every clause carrying a touch of irony
the profession was genuine as far as it went and is granted its due, but availed nothing because not made in truth and righteousness
they were Israelites in name and not in truth, professing the true religion by one act standing for all

debates.question: What is meant by staying themselves upon the God of Israel?

positions.view: not sincere belief but empty confidence: hypocrites intoxicated by unfounded assurance, boasting that God will not cast off his people as if he wished to encourage their wickedness
not a true faith but a vain confidence
leaning on the Lord and boasting of the covenant, so that they reckoned themselves happy and very great in having such a God

outliers.reading: Alone turns the boast of the holy city on his own contemporaries, at those who call themselves fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God while strangers to both.
Alone finds the closing title a threat rather than a comfort, added so that men sheltering falsely under the name might know God loses nothing of his authority by being misrepresented.

themes: Hear ye this, O house of Jacob, which are called by the name of Israel, and are come forth out of the waters of Judah, which swear by the name of the Lord, and make mention of the God of Israel, but not in truth, nor in righteousness.
For they call themselves of the holy city, and stay themselves upon the God of Israel; The Lord of hosts is his name.

3.pericope_label: I have declared the former things from the beginning: I have shewed thee new things, even hidden things

schools.summary: Counts this the seventh appeal to foreknowledge and notes it is now aimed at the little faith of Judah rather than the no-faith of the heathen, and explains the reserve by which what lay from the first in the mind of God is only now disclosed.
Says God dealt more liberally than he need have done, distinguishes a sinew that can be bent from one that cannot, and answers why idols are mentioned at all to a people professing one God.
Grounds the clearer demonstrations in the nation's unbelief, works the imperative textually, and reads the creating of the new things as a bringing to light.

debates.question: What are the new things now declared?

positions.view: the deliverance out of Babylon by the promised conqueror, secret things until now unknown
something further off: that conquest belongs with the former things, and the new lie in a more distant future

debates.question: Why did God foretell so much in advance?

positions.view: because their depravity was otherwise incurable; he acted more liberally towards them than he ought to have done, though the chief use of doctrine belongs to believers who submit gently
because he knew the nation unbelieving, and so gave clearer demonstrations of his nature and providence
because he foresaw not only the conquests of the deliverer but the obduracy of the delivered, still inclined to credit another god

outliers.reading: Alone gives a reason for the long reserve, that the people had been unprepared to receive the truth and in their state it would only have increased their condemnation.
Alone takes the imperative as a duty laid on the hearer rather than a claim about the speaker: since the Lord has spoken, it is our business to examine and attend, and pleading ignorance is vain.

themes: I have declared the former things from the beginning; and they went forth out of my mouth, and I shewed them; I did them suddenly, and they came to pass.
Because I knew that thou art obstinate, and thy neck is an iron sinew, and thy brow brass;

I have even from the beginning declared it to thee; before it came to pass I shewed it thee: lest thou shouldest say, Mine idol hath done them, and my graven image, and my molten image, hath commanded them.
Thou hast heard, see all this; and will not ye declare it? I have shewed thee new things from this time, even hidden things, and thou didst not know them.
They are created now, and not from the beginning; even before the day when thou heardest them not; lest thou shouldest say, Behold, I knew them.
Yea, thou heardest not; yea, thou knewest not; yea, from that time that thine ear was not opened: for I knew that thou wouldest deal very treacherously, and wast called a transgressor from the womb.

9.pericope_label: For my name sake will I defer mine anger: behold, I have refined thee, but not with silver

schools.summary: Gives two reasons for the sparing, that destruction would have made God seem capricious and that the name stands for a character willing to save; and suspects the refining figure rests on a lost process of ancient metallurgy.

Finds two uses in the announcement, support during the captivity and humbling after it, presses the free character of the remission against the schoolmen, and says that silver at least has something pure in it where we have only chaff.
Reads the whole as vindication of the divine name, restores a displaced particle, prefers tried to chosen, and observes that silver is kept in the fire until no dross remains.
Renders the deferring as a stifling of anger, and makes the furnace the place where God chooses, since affliction is no bar to his choice but subservient to his purpose.

debates.question: What does refining not with silver mean?

positions.view: not as silver is refined, which leaves no dross at all and would have consumed them altogether
silver contains something pure, but in us nothing would be found but chaff, so God measures the trial to what we can bear and by his Spirit makes it profitable
the discipline was deliberately less fierce than a refiner's fire, though the figure may rest on some unknown ancient process
several renderings are possible: not in a furnace of silver, in a furnace of poverty, not into silver, or not for the sake of silver

debates.question: Is the next verb chosen or tried?

positions.view: tried, on the authority of a manuscript and the eastern versions
chosen, and the point stands: affliction is no bar to God's choice but subservient to his purpose, and many have been made choice vessels in the furnace
chosen, and a second choosing, of a people God had in a manner rejected

outliers.reading: Alone turns the verse against the schoolmen, arguing that since remission here is free and for God's name's sake, the distinction collapses which refuses to call the remission of punishment undeserved on the ground that satisfaction has been made.
Alone answers the implied question why so guilty a people was spared twice over, once from what the nations would have concluded and once from what the divine name as a symbol of character requires.

themes: For my name’s sake will I defer mine anger, and for my praise will I refrain for thee, that I cut thee not off.
Behold, I have refined thee, but not with silver; I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction.
For mine own sake, even for mine own sake, will I do it: for how should my name be polluted? and I will not give my glory unto another.

12.pericope_label: I am he, I am the first, I also am the last: mine hand hath laid the foundation of the earth

schools.summary: Places the passage as a condensed epitome of the whole preceding argument, and finds in the word for the beloved an allusion making the foreign conqueror a second David.

Reads the changed address as a father owning the son he has just called a bastard, preserves a distinction about which hand made the earth, and refuses to labour a verb that may mean either measured or upheld.
Repairs the text twice over, identifies the beloved plainly from an old Greek version, and reads the standing up of the hosts as a readiness to execute commands.

debates.question: Who is summoned to assemble and hear?

positions.view: the worshippers of idols, as in the earlier challenge
the Jews, since the unbelieving have no ears and are not invited, and a people to whom God revealed himself above all nations was the less excusable

debates.question: What does the verb about the heavens mean?

positions.view: either measured or upheld indifferently: on the first an amazing wisdom that set the expanse neither nearer the earth nor further than order requires, on the second a power holding the mass in motion without tottering
spanned, the right hand doing the more honourable work while the left laid the earth's foundation

outliers.reading: Alone hears in the word for the beloved an allusion to the name of Israel's great king, so that the foreign conqueror is to be as a second David, beloved of the Lord.

Alone explains the reversal by a domestic figure: as a father rebuking his son may call him a bastard and afterwards own him, so God regards his own calling, which no ingratitude of men can set aside.

themes: Hearken unto me, O Jacob and Israel, my called; I am he; I am the first, I also am the last.
Mine hand also hath laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand hath spanned the heavens: when I call unto them, they stand up together.
All ye, assemble yourselves, and hear; which among them hath declared these things? The Lord hath loved him: he will do his pleasure on Babylon, and his arm shall be on the Chaldeans.
I, even I, have spoken; yea, I have called him: I have brought him, and he shall make his way prosperous.

16.pericope_label: Come ye near unto me, hear ye this: and now the Lord GOD, and his Spirit, hath sent me

schools.summary: Reads the address as made to Israel, paraphrases the sequence of thought against the dark ambiguous speech of heathen oracles, and records the rival constructions of the closing clause without settling among them.

Takes the distance to be of the heart rather than of space, makes drawing near a work of grace, and rejects both the christological and the prophetic readings of the sending in favour of God as the speaker.
Suspects the summons is addressed to the nations, turns an adverb into a verb so that the clause reads I had decreed it, and finds in the sent one a prophet who is also a type of Christ.

Requires the hearer to come as near as he can, recalls a God who spoke publicly from Sinai and in the assemblies, and finds the Spirit named here as a person distinct from Father and Son with authority to send prophets.

debates.question: Who says: and now the Lord GOD, and his Spirit, hath sent me?

positions.view: Christ, the great prophet, the Spirit appearing as a person distinct from Father and Son with divine authority to send
Isaiah, who is also a type of Christ, so that the words may respect him too
the prophet, appearing abruptly in his own person at the close and perhaps speaking throughout, though other constructions refer the words to the servant of the Lord

neither: the application to Christ is a forced interpretation the prophet never meant, and the application to the prophet is unsuitable, since such a discourse could not be spoken by a man; God himself is the speaker

debates.question: Who is called to draw near?

positions.view: the idolatrous nations, a manuscript adding the words O ye nations after the summons, which is probably genuine since these verses reproach their gods
Israel, or the Jews, called to attend and reproached for ingratitude

outliers.reading: Alone refuses both of the standard readings of the sending, and makes the drawing near a work of grace, since the distance was one of the heart and we are never prepared to close it unless God leads us.
Alone takes the word usually rendered there as a verb rather than an adverb, so that the clause becomes I had decreed it, and dates the decree to the planning of the conqueror's expedition.

themes: Come ye near unto me, hear ye this; I have not spoken in secret from the beginning; from the time that it was, there am I: and now the Lord God, and his Spirit, hath sent me.

17.pericope_label: O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments: go ye forth of Babylon, there is no peace unto the wicked

schools.summary: Reads teaching to profit against the ordinary desire to make a good investment, identifies the river as the Euphrates and the gravel as the creatures of the sea, and answers the literalist objection about the water from the rock.

Anticipates the complaint that a preventable disease earns the physician little thanks, hears a father deploring his children's ruin, and warns against pressing the wish into the secret counsel of God.
Places the blame squarely, since they knew their duty and cannot plead ignorance, and defends the prophet's parabolic style against a commentator who wanted the miracles recorded.

debates.question: How should the water from the rock be understood?

positions.view: parabolically: the style runs from the first verse of the book to the last, and to want such miracles recorded of the return is to miss it entirely
symbolically: a dead prosaic literalism looks for a record, but the water from the rock is as ever the symbol of spiritual refreshment
as a recollection of the exodus, against those who invent miracles never performed, not through ignorance but presumption
as a supply actually made, to the returning exiles as to Israel in the wilderness, and afterwards to the apostles and to the people of God in this world

debates.question: What is the force of the closing line about the wicked?

positions.view: repunctuate it, so that God says to the wicked there is no peace, shutting hypocrites out of promises they would otherwise claim
an implied condition on all God's gifts, since freedom and home were no real blessing to those unworthy of them
an explication appended to the promised peace, declaring that wicked men should not enjoy the benefit of that mercy

outliers.reading: Alone closes a door on the wish, warning that it is foolish to press into the secret counsel and ask why the efficacy of the Spirit was not added to the outward word, since the verse speaks not of power but of reproof.
Alone hears in these two verses the sigh that has come from the heart of every true teacher comparing what men are with what they might have been.

themes: Thus saith the Lord, thy Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel; I am the Lord thy God which teacheth thee to profit, which leadeth thee by the way that thou shouldest go.
O that thou hadst hearkened to my commandments! then had thy peace been as a river, and thy righteousness as the waves of the sea:
Thy seed also had been as the sand, and the offspring of thy bowels like the gravel thereof; his name should not have been cut off nor destroyed from before me.
Go ye forth of Babylon, flee ye from the Chaldeans, with a voice of singing declare ye, tell this, utter it even to the end of the earth; say ye, The Lord hath redeemed his servant Jacob.
And they thirsted not when he led them through the deserts: he caused the waters to flow out of the rock for them: he clave the rock also, and the waters gushed out.
There is no peace, saith the Lord, unto the wicked.
